title: [LAB] Daily simulated-developer feedback for BogKit
body:
Note: directly inspired by: https://gist.github.com/VictorTaelin/d632f46aa55e561d3cd2c43c66f2813e

## Purpose

This long-lived draft PR is the evidence archive and discussion thread for a daily simulated-developer feedback lab.

Every run gives two fresh developer personas realistic existing-software problems before they inspect BogKit. They begin with the public onboarding surface, build the smallest meaningful integration or no-fit reproducer, run it, and record the complete friction trail. A separate skeptical reviewer reproduces material claims and rejects unsupported or bloated recommendations.

## Boundaries

- Daily changes stay under `developer-simulation/`.
- The automation never changes BogKit core or existing examples automatically.
- A trial may conclude that BogKit is not a fit.
- Generated data, credentials, databases, build output, and unjustified large dependencies are never archived.
- Findings remain proposals until a maintainer explicitly approves separate implementation work.
- This PR is intentionally long-lived and should remain draft rather than being merged.

## Reporting

- Each day gets one immutable PR comment containing the verified report.
- One rolling dashboard comment tracks coverage, recurring evidence, confirmed defects, no-fit signals, and candidate improvements.
- A suggestion becomes a candidate only after two independent trials or one serious reproducible correctness defect.

## Inaugural run

The first two trials cover:

1. A PostgreSQL purchase-approval audit timeline requiring one transaction and role-protected immutability.
2. Offline warehouse scanner reconciliation under duplicate, reordered, interrupted, and conflicting uploads.

Both produced runnable archives. Neither justified adding BogKit to the specified production architecture. The repeated, evidence-backed improvement is a concise onboarding capability matrix describing embedded storage, transaction, single-writer, and component boundaries.

## Validation

- 15 inaugural trial tests passed.
- Strict lint passed with warnings denied.
- All archived Rust sources passed formatting checks.
- Both demonstrations ran successfully.
- The 20,000-operation synthetic threshold passed.
- All 45 existing BogKit unit and documentation tests passed.
- A skeptical review reproduced the major claims and removed overclaims and speculative API proposals.

See `developer-simulation/README.md` for the protocol and `developer-simulation/reports/2026-07-28.md` for the first full report.

title: add MUDGarden, a persistent gardening MUD built on Fold
body:
## Summary

MUDGarden is a persistent gardening MUD over SSH. Human players and model-planned residents share one serialized world and the same command, permission, and mutation paths.

This is a BogKit hackathon submission in the agent support and novel interface
/ gaming categories.

## Changes

- Adds the complete `examples/mudgarden` crate and documentation.
- Uses Fold to persist the keyed world source and incrementally maintain actors, rooms, gardens, plants, schedules, ecology, species aggregates, and moisture percentiles.
- Adds SSH play, a browser field console, multi-player test sessions, editable content, resident action traces, Docker packaging, and Railway configuration.
- Updates `Cargo.lock` for the new example dependencies.

## How did I test?

- `cargo test --locked -p mudgarden` — 63 passed
- `cargo clippy --locked -p mudgarden --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --package mudgarden --check`
- `bash -n examples/mudgarden/scripts/*.sh`
- `docker build --check --file examples/mudgarden/Dockerfile .`

### what you built

A persistent shared gardening world where plants, weather, ecology, people, and autonomous residents continue changing between connections. Fold is the source of truth and incrementally maintains the materialized views that make world reads, due schedules, ecological stress, spatial lookups, and aggregate statistics cheap.

title: séance: time-travel repo search
body:
## Hackathon submission

### category

pick **one**:

- [ ] agent support
- [x] performance
- [ ] novel interface / gaming

### team

- **project name:** séance
- **team / author name(s):** Taylor Hodge
- **contact (optional):** twitter.com/jtaylorhodge

### what you built

Séance is time-travel search for git repositories. It shows a repository
at any commit in its history. You move a slider. The search indexes
follow. You can search each version of the repository in three ways:
keyword (BM25), semantic (ese vectors), and hybrid (reciprocal-rank
fusion). A header shows live statistics for the version on screen.

We measured séance against SQLite FTS5 plus a flat vector scan on one
workload: sqlite.git, 23,525 commits, a 2,000-commit walk, the same
queries, the same content rules, the same ese vectors. The full method
and tables are in `examples/seance/bench/RESULTS.md`.

**Headline results:**

| operation | séance (bog) | sqlite fts5 + flat scan | factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| semantic top-10 | **68µs** | 43.3ms | **637×** |
| hybrid keyword+semantic+rrf | **359µs** | 43.4ms | **121×** |
| keyword top-10 | 0.3ms | 0.2ms | parity |
| stats read (also as-of any commit) | **<1µs** | 60µs | **60×** |
| warp into a visited era, all views | 61ms | 10.8ms (text index only) | see tradeoffs |

**How each part of bogkit causes these gains:**

- **fold** holds seven materialized views correct through one delta
  stream: BM25 postings, the HNSW graph, a document table, counts,
  per-extension aggregates, line statistics, and a temporal index.
  Retraction is the mechanism that makes time travel exact: a move of
  the cursor applies one diff, forward or backward, and every view
  rolls with it. One commit step costs 22ms (p50). No view is ever
  rebuilt. Fold's `KeyedRanked` sink powers the "chronicle": its
  order-preserving score encoding makes "this file, this stat, as of
  commit T" a single bounded seek — 1–3µs across all 23,525 commits,
  from a 16MB store, with zero writes to scrub.
- **ese** makes embeddings a pure function of file content. This lets
  séance store the vector inside each fold record, so retraction never
  computes an embedding again. Batch encoding with the rayon feature
  embeds a full 2,220-file tree in ~95ms. The 68µs semantic query
  above includes the query embedding.
- **anny** gives true deletion: a removed vector repairs the graph
  instead of leaving a tombstone. Recall does not decay across the
  2,000-commit churn walk. This PR adds graph serialization to anny
  (`write_to`/`read_from`, bit-faithful) and a fast-load path to
  fold's Hnsw sink. A warp then restores the graph at memory
  bandwidth instead of re-inserting every vector — that is the
  difference between a 1.5s warp and a 61ms warp.
- **fold's persistent stores + APFS clonefile** give checkpoint-clone
  time travel: a full snapshot of all seven views costs one CoW clone
  (10–40ms at any store size). Visited eras become immutable masters.
  A return visit clones a master and opens it in tens of
  milliseconds, semantic search included.

**Where SQLite wins, and why (tradeoffs we measured and accept):**

- Apply: 2.3ms vs 22ms p50, 10× for SQLite. SQLite maintains one
  index. Bog maintains seven views and computes an embedding for each
  changed file on every write.
- Cold 10,000-commit jump: 590ms vs 3,275ms, 5.5× for SQLite. Same
  cause. The checkpoint-clone design exists for this reason: séance
  pays this cost once per era, then returns in 61ms.
- Snapshot create and warp: 9.9ms and 10.8ms for SQLite. A
  single-file database copies very well — this surprised us and we
  report it. But the SQLite warp restores a text index only. The bog
  warp restores semantic search too. A semantic query at the SQLite
  destination still costs 43ms.
- The rule the numbers show: bog pays at write time and wins where
  reads multiply.

### how to run

```bash
# from repo root
cargo run -p seance -- /path/to/any/git/repo
# then open http://localhost:3333
```

- First start of a large repository: a few seconds to materialize HEAD,
  plus a background chronicle build (~11s for sqlite.git; the app is
  usable during the build). Later starts resume from a checkpoint in
  ~40ms.
- Set `SEANCE_PORT` to change the port.
- Correctness check: `cargo run -p seance -- <repo> --probe "query"`
  walks HEAD → first commit → HEAD and fails if any view diverges.
- Benchmarks: `cargo run -p seance -- <repo> --bench-walk 2000
  --dump-vecs /tmp/vecs.json`, then
  `python3 examples/seance/bench/bench.py sqlite <repo> 2000 --vecs
  /tmp/vecs.json`, then the `summary` and `capsummary` subcommands.
  No Python dependencies.
- macOS/APFS gives O(1) checkpoint clones. Other filesystems fall back
  to full copies.

### demo / notes

- Benchmark report: `examples/seance/bench/RESULTS.md`.
- Demo path: search at HEAD; drag the slider (live playback, ~20ms per
  commit, results update as history replays); fling to a distant era
  (teleport); dwell (the era becomes a checkpoint); return (61ms warp,
  semantic search intact). The header updates in microseconds from the
  chronicle during every jump.
- Findings for the bogkit team, found by the probe and the benchmark:
  1. `Bm25` corrupts term frequencies when one transaction retracts
     and re-inserts the same document. Séance works around this with
     separate retract and insert transactions (`goto`, main.rs).
  2. Posting keyspaces need periodic compaction: query latency grows
     ~50× per 1,000 commits of churn without it, and stays flat with
     a `major_compact` every 200 commits.
  3. anny graph serialization (this PR) removes the only O(n) cost on
     store open.

title: tompkins-audio-search — a searchable, multimodal memory of a park, on fold
body:
## Hackathon submission

### category

pick **one**:

- [ ] agent support
- [ ] performance
- [x] novel interface / gaming

### team

- **project name:** tompkins-audio-search
- **team / author name(s):** Dan Brewster
- **contact (optional):** dnbrwstr@gmail.com

### what you built

A searchable, multimodal memory of Tompkins Square Park. Ask for spoken words, weather, city sounds or bird species and land on the moment the archive remembers — on one wall-clock timeline spanning the whole corpus, not a file browser.

The interface is the timeline. Every stream in the archive is placed on a single 53.8-day axis (108 placements, 3 lanes where microphones overlap), search hits are highlighted on it, and clicking anywhere resolves to playable audio. Playback is the timeline; there is no separate player.

**How it uses bog-kit.** One `fold::stream::KeyedStream<RecordKey, Record>` carries all five record types into a 12-way tuple fan-out, so a single `upsert` atomically updates the acoustic vector index, transcript BM25 postings, the transcript embedding graph, bird labels and embeddings, the per-stream time index, the species vocabulary and the coverage views — and one `remove` retracts it from all of them.

That guarantee is the reason for the design, and it's exercised on real data: dropping a 30,668-record stream cleared every index in one operation, verified from outside (species vocabulary → 0, bird and speech queries → empty, playable hours 35.83 → 23.81, no orphans).

- `anny` backs three typed HNSW indexes — CLAP 512-d, `ese` 512-d, BirdNET 1024-d
- `ese` embeds transcripts *inside* the pipeline, which retraction requires: it must be a pure function of the text so cancelling re-derives the same vector
- `terminal::KeyedRanked` range scans are what make "a bird while it is raining" mean conjunction *in time* — it narrows 77 episodes to 1
- Record keys are stable across reprocessing (`model_version` lives in the record body, not the key), so re-running a model *replaces* evidence instead of accumulating a stale copy

Inference never holds the write lock: Python workers stage checksummed batches and hand them to the single store owner for a short commit. `anny`'s HNSW state is `Rc<RefCell<_>>` so `Store` isn't `Send`, which forces exactly the single-owner thread `fold`'s single-writer discipline wants anyway.

### how to run

```bash
# from repo root
cargo test -p tompkins-audio-search   # 92 tests, no data or credentials needed
cargo run -p tompkins-audio-search    # subcommands: manifest / timeline / commit / serve / forget
```

**What a judge can actually run:** the test suite, standalone. It's the honest entry point — most of the interesting behaviour is pinned there (PTS wraparound across 358 simulated hours, gap handling, atomic retraction, rank fusion, episode grouping, conjunction).

The ingestion path needs read access to a private Oda S3 bucket plus a local cross-reference catalog, so it isn't reproducible outside this machine. `examples/tompkins-audio-search/README.md` documents the full pipeline, and `docs/adr/` records the decisions.

### demo / notes

Built against ~47.6 h of real archive audio. Some findings that shaped it:

- **The playlists are live sliding windows, not VOD** (~12 segments, no `ENDLIST`), so they can't enumerate a 358-hour stream. Order comes from object numbering instead.
- **`EXTINF` isn't imprecise, it's wrong.** It advertises 93-frame segments; decoded PTS shows 91/92/93/94. Trusting it drifts **−690 s over 24 h** and −2.87 h over the full stream. Time is accumulated in 90 kHz ticks so rounding can't reintroduce it.
- **PTS wraps every ~26.5 h**; the longest stream crosses that ~13 times. Unhandled, a late seek lands hours away.
- **Nothing carries `EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME`**, so no wall clock is exact. The UI says so on every view: exact within a stream, approximate between streams.
- **CLAP zero-shot tags needed per-label calibration.** Scored by softmax, "bicycle" fired on 42% of windows and no window came out untagged — a per-window normalisation can't express "none of these apply". Calibrated against each label's own corpus distribution, the same tag lands at 0.13%.
- **k-NN always returns k results**, so a query for something absent still filled a page. Untagged hits measured 0.005–0.043 similarity against the 0.25 a tag requires; there's now a floor, and the number is shown.

**Known issue, documented rather than hidden:** large stretches of the archive are phase-inverted (L/R correlation to −0.95). The workers decoded with `-ac 1` = `(L+R)/2`, which *cancels* that — 9.3 dB lost, the speech band down from 6.6% to 0.01%. The first diagnosis was also wrong: scanning through the same downmix reported 87/96 assets as dead audio, where a single channel put it at 0/12. Fixed in this PR; the committed indexes predate the fix and need re-running.

Milestone 5 (the evaluation gate) is **not built**, so nothing here has been validated by listening. That's the honest gap.

title: bog-bench — a benchmark harness for agent tooling, on fold
body:
## Hackathon submission

### category

- [ ] agent support
- [x] performance
- [ ] novel interface / gaming

### team

- **project name:** bog-bench
- **team / author name(s):** mrojas54 (built with Claude Code as a pair)
- **contact (optional):** via this PR

### what you built

**Fold one newly completed session into persistent aggregate views without
rescanning prior sessions; three local five-trial measurements kept append cost
in the same tens-of-milliseconds range across 51–801 sessions.**

![bog-bench application and fold architecture, including exact retraction, isolated windows, and local benchmark measurements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrojas54/bogkit/bog-bench/examples/bog-bench/assets/bog-bench-overview.webp)

bog-bench turns Claude Code tool calls into persistent `fold` materialized
views: corpus totals, per-tool rows, explicit-error and unknown-outcome counts,
per-session rows, and an exact counted bag of the ingested calls.

The exact-call bag fixes the two shipping blockers identified in final review:

- `demo` now owns a process-unique scratch database, while no-argument
  invocation prints help without opening persistent state;
- transcript identity is the canonical path, growing files reconcile by
  atomically replacing their prior stored snapshot, and `retract` removes only
  that stored snapshot instead of reparsing possibly changed contents.

Ordinary ingest updates persistent aggregate views from deltas without
rescanning prior sessions. Reconciliation touches the selected session
snapshot. `window` is a separate full event-time replay into a scratch stream.

Unmatched calls are `Unknown`, not successful. `ERROR%` is explicit errors over
known outcomes, malformed/unmatched input emits parser diagnostics, and `CHARS`
means normalized joined-result characters—not raw payload bytes or total model
context cost.

The corrected six-branch architecture and persistence boundaries are in
[`examples/bog-bench/README.md`](examples/bog-bench/README.md#materialized-views).

### how to run

```bash
cargo run -p bog-bench --             # help; no state mutation
cargo run -p bog-bench -- demo        # isolated fixtures
cargo test -p bog-bench               # 19 debug-build tests
cargo test --release -p bog-bench     # 18 release-build tests
```

`demo` ingests one fixture session, appends another, then retracts it:

```text
== appended session-b — views moved, nothing rescanned ==
9 tool calls · 3 explicit errors among 9 known outcomes · 0 unknown outcomes

  TOOL                        CALLS  ERROR    UNK  ERROR%       CHARS     ~TOK
  Read                            3      0      0      0%       67600    16900
  Bash                            4      3      0     75%        6640     1660
  Grep                            1      0      0      0%        3300      825
  Edit                            1      0      0      0%         180       45

== retracted session-b — every counter rolled back ==
5 tool calls · 1 explicit error among 5 known outcomes · 0 unknown outcomes
```

`Grep` disappears because it existed only in the stored snapshot that was
retracted. `recent`, `show`, `ingest`, `retract`, `bench`, `window`, and `reset`
read the local corpus under `~/.claude/projects`.

### benchmark evidence

```bash
cargo run -p bog-bench -- bench 800 5
```

Each trial compares total calls, explicit-error and unknown counts, every
per-tool row, every per-session row, and the exact-call bag before reporting
timings. A mismatch exits non-zero.

Local environment: `macos/aarch64`, debug profile, 8 logical CPUs, five trials
per corpus size.

| corpus | arriving calls | incremental total median (min–max, σ) | full rescan total median (min–max, σ) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 51 sessions | 290 | 32.5 ms (29.0–37.2, 2.7) | 680.9 ms (601.4–717.2, 42.0) |
| 201 sessions | 291 | 40.7 ms (35.8–70.9, 14.2) | 749.1 ms (704.9–1,050.0, 133.2) |
| 801 sessions | 292 | 48.6 ms (38.4–50.8, 4.6) | 1,052.2 ms (908.6–1,154.0, 82.4) |

The selected private corpus was live, so the newest transcript grew slightly
between commands. These runs show incremental work remaining in the same
tens-of-milliseconds range while full replay grew across this local range. They
are measurements, not a durable complexity guarantee; other machines, stores,
corpora, profiles, and workloads need their own repeated trials.

The comparison arm is a full-rescan batch design; incremental or cached systems
can also avoid rescans but must supply their own persistence and retraction
semantics. There is no cross-engine throughput comparison.

This output could support a future CI policy. The current CLI reports metrics
but does not define a baseline, threshold, or pass/fail gate.

### verification

Full local code gate at head `4682c1f`:

- scoped `rustfmt --check`;
- `cargo clippy -p bog-bench --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings`;
- 19 debug and 18 release `bog-bench` tests;
- `cargo test --workspace` and `cargo test --workspace --release`, including
  doctests;
- a concurrent two-process regression proving scratch test stores no longer
  collide.

The docs-only visual head `950807d` separately passed `git diff --check`,
a 1672×941 WebP inspection, and `cargo test -p bog-bench` (19 tests).

Repository CI now runs the workspace test suite in both debug and release
profiles.

Seventeen tests are deterministic and fixture-based. Two local-corpus smoke
checks return early when no corpus is present.

In one private 114-session corpus, the parser recorded 2,668 tool calls, 100
carrying explicit error flags. One browser-automation tool had 5 flagged errors
across 10 calls and averaged approximately 4,200 normalized result characters
per call. These observations are not independently reproducible from this PR.

title: Area denial: a location-based team game built on fold
body:
## Summary
- Adds `mmo-cs`, a location-based "area denial" team game (spec in `project-idea.md`): two teams stream GPS location from the browser, and fold maintains a live per-team scoreboard (roster size, in-bounds presence) over a websocket, following `examples/chat`'s ingest-thread/watch-channel architecture.
- Win conditions: instant elimination when a team is confirmed swept from the battleground (debounced against flaky GPS), or a 3-hour timeout decided by in-bounds percentage with a headcount tiebreak.
- Battleground catalog is a curated extract of real Brooklyn/Queens parks from NYC Open Data's public "Parks Properties" dataset (Foursquare's OS Places dataset, named in the original spec, now requires a gated Hugging Face account/token).
- `fold::pipeline::Keyed<K, V>` now derives `Serialize`/`Deserialize`, needed for `Retain` to wrap a `KeyedStream`'s root `Keyed` type directly.
